content.title: About
content.content: A burrito is a traditional Mexican dish consisting of a large soft wheat tortilla wrapped around a variety of fillings such as meat, beans, rice, cheese, vegetables, and sauces. The NFS (No Fillings Specified) version refers to a basic set of ingredients without additional toppings.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Burritos first appeared in the northern regions of Mexico in the early 20th century.
The word “burrito” translates to “little donkey,” though the exact origin of the name is uncertain.
Burritos became popular in the United States in the 1970s thanks to fast‑food chains like Taco Bell.
Traditional Mexican burritos are usually modest in size, while U.S. versions are often oversized.
The NFS option is frequently used in menus to accommodate vegetarians and people with dietary restrictions.

items.title: Balanced macronutrients
items.content: A burrito that includes meat, beans, and rice provides protein, complex carbohydrates, and a modest amount of fat.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Beans and whole‑grain tortillas are rich in dietary fiber, which supports digestion.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Meat and whole grains supply B1, B3, and B6 vitamins important for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Burritos contain iron, magnesium, and zinc, which help maintain immune function and energy production.

items.title: Nutrient density
items.content: When portioned reasonably, a burrito can be a satisfying and nutrient‑dense meal.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Large burritos can be high in calories and fat, which may be undesirable for weight management.

items.title: Sodium levels
items.content: Sauces and processed ingredients often contain a lot of salt, posing a risk for people with hypertension.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Burritos may contain dairy, gluten, and soy, which can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Improperly cooked meat or beans can harbor harmful bacteria or toxins.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Burritos are typically served hot. Slice them in half, add fresh veggies, salsa, guacamole, or sour cream. For a lighter option, choose a whole‑grain tortilla and lean meat or plant‑based protein.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store a prepared burrito in an airtight container in the refrigerator for 2‑3 days. For freezing, wrap tightly in plastic film and place in a freezer bag; it keeps up to 2 months. Reheat in the microwave or oven before eating.

content.title: About
content.content: Fruit‑filled crepes are thin, delicate pancakes made from eggs, milk and flour, rolled around a sweet fruit filling that may include fresh or canned fruits, a touch of sugar and butter. They work well as a light breakfast, dessert or snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Crepes have ancient roots, with early versions known in Roman and Chinese cuisines.
Typical fruit fillings include apples, berries, peaches, pineapple, and even exotic mango.
In France, thin crepes are a classic dish often simply called “crêpes.”
The recipe can be adapted for dietary needs by using whole‑grain or gluten‑free flours.
Traditionally crepes are dusted with powdered sugar or drizzled with fruit sauce.

items.title: Rich in vitamins
items.content: Fruit fillings provide vitamin C, vitamin A and other antioxidants that support the immune system.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Both the fruit and whole‑grain flour contribute dietary fiber, aiding digestion and satiety.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: When butter is used sparingly, crepes remain a light dish with modest saturated‑fat content.

items.title: Quick energy
items.content: Carbohydrates from the batter and fruit quickly replenish glycogen stores, useful before physical activity.

items.title: Heart‑friendly potassium
items.content: Fruits supply potassium, which helps maintain healthy blood pressure.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional flour contains gluten, which can trigger reactions in people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Fruit fillings are often sweetened, which may be a concern for individuals managing diabetes or sugar intake.

items.title: Additives in ready‑made fillings
items.content: Some pre‑made fruit mixes contain preservatives and artificial flavors.

items.title: Burn risk
items.content: Both batter and filling can be hot right after cooking; allow them to cool before serving.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve crepes warm, rolled or folded into triangles. They can be eaten by hand or with a fork. Enhance the filling with whipped cream, yogurt, honey, or a sprinkle of nuts.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked crepes in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. Store the fruit filling separately to prevent the crepes from becoming soggy. For longer storage, freeze crepes in sealed bags at –18 °C and reheat in a microwave or skillet before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: A sweet roll without frosting is a soft sponge roll soaked with fragrant syrup and filled with a light cream or fruit purée. It has no icing, which keeps the texture airy and the flavor pure.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The roll tradition began in Europe in the 19th century and quickly spread worldwide.
Sweet rolls are a popular treat for birthdays, holidays, and celebrations.
Skipping the frosting makes the roll easier to prepare and helps control sugar levels.
Fillings can range from berry, nut, chocolate to creamy cheese variations.
The roll can be sliced thinly and served as bite‑size desserts.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: The sponge cake provides carbohydrates that supply quick energy.

items.title: Contains protein
items.content: Creamy fillings often use cottage cheese, yogurt, or eggs, adding protein.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Flour and eggs are rich in B1, B2, and B6 vitamins, supporting metabolism.

items.title: Mineral content
items.content: Depending on the filling, the roll can provide calcium, magnesium, and potassium.

items.title: Moderate fat level
items.content: When the filling is made with low‑fat dairy, the overall fat content remains modest.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional sponge cake uses wheat flour, which is unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Syrup and sweet fillings raise sugar levels, so those with diabetes should limit portions.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Even without frosting, the roll remains calorie‑dense due to the cake and cream.

items.title: Food intolerances
items.content: Fillings may contain dairy, nuts, or eggs, which can trigger allergies.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the roll in individual slices, optionally dusted with powdered sugar or fresh berries. It can be eaten with hands or using a knife and fork.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the roll in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer storage, refrigerate up to 5 days or freeze for up to 2 months.

yogurt-greek-nonfat-milk-fruit.title: Greek Nonfat Milk Yogurt with Fruit

content.title: About
content.content: Greek yogurt is a thick, strained yogurt. This version is made with nonfat milk and contains fruit pieces, making it low‑calorie, high in protein, and rich in vitamins.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Greek yogurt contains two to three times more protein than regular yogurt.
Nonfat milk retains most nutrients while contributing virtually no fat.
Fruit additions often include berries, peach, or mango, boosting vitamin C content.
Traditional Greek yogurt is strained through cheesecloth for 2‑4 hours.
Greek yogurt is frequently used as a substitute for sour cream or mayonnaise in recipes.

items.title: High protein content
items.content: Protein supports muscle maintenance and promotes satiety.

items.title: Low fat
items.content: Using nonfat milk makes the product suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Probiotics
items.content: Live cultures in yogurt help maintain a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: Fruit adds vitamin C, potassium, and antioxidants, while milk provides calcium and vitamin D.

items.title: Immune support
items.content: The combination of probiotics and vitamins can strengthen the immune system.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Even though the milk is nonfat, it still contains lactose, which may cause discomfort for sensitive individuals.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Some people may react to casein or whey proteins.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Fruit pieces can raise sugar levels; choose unsweetened versions if monitoring glucose.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Yogurt is acidic and may aggravate those with high stomach acidity.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the yogurt as a snack, blend it into smoothies, use it as a base for sauces, dressings, or desserts. It pairs well with nuts, honey, or whole‑grain cereals.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the yogurt in the refrigerator at 1‑4 °C. After opening, consume within 5‑7 days. Do not freeze, as the texture may change.
